# The 20 Percent Plan Is Gone. But That Alone Does Not Explain Price Moves

What is a little interesting here is that the day after a plan with a clear figure—20 percent—was proposed, the proposal itself took a different shape.

On July 13, Mr. Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20 percent reimbursement fee on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz, to cover the cost of ensuring its safety. The next day, he posted that the plan would be replaced with trade and investment deals involving Gulf countries and the United States. He said the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

stage2_results.local_context:
What is a little interesting here is that the day after a plan with a clear figure—20 percent—was proposed, the proposal itself took a different shape.

On July 13, Mr. Trump posted that the United States would seek a 20 percent reimbursement fee on all cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz, to cover the cost of ensuring its safety. The next day, he posted that the plan would be replaced with trade and investment deals involving Gulf countries and the United States. He said the decision was based on “very productive talks” with Middle Eastern leaders.

But the movement in oil prices cannot be explained by the fee plan alone. On July 13, Brent futures rose $7.29 a barrel and settled at $83.30. Reports linked the rise to a naval blockade of Iran, which was expected to begin the next day, and to concerns about energy shipments through the strait. We cannot say that the 20 percent plan alone caused prices to rise.
